text.content:
“Clarity over chance. Choice over chaos.”

The Mastery System is a roleplaying game designed for heroes who grow through struggle, discovery, and the choices they make at the table. It is not bound by rigid classes or endless charts of bonuses. Instead, it focuses on clarity, cinematic action, and player-driven mastery in a world where success comes not from luck, but from understanding the system, making smart decisions, and taking responsibility for every choice. What sets it apart is how it handles power: it is classless, modular, and mathematically transparent. Your strength does not come from arbitrary level spikes or hidden feature packages — it comes from Mastery Ranks, Stones, your chosen Powers, and the way you combine them.

Mastery Ranks keep heroes on the same curve.
No one falls behind because their class “comes online later.” No one runs away with the game because of a single feature spike. Progression is consistent and comparable, built on a foundation that can be measured, tuned, and proven, not guessed. In the Mastery System, players are not at the mercy of hidden mechanics: they see the numbers, shape their fate, and own their triumphs and failures alike.

At its heart, the system rests on a few core ideas:

  • Attributes Define Capability
    Each point in an Attribute adds one die to its Pool. Attributes determine how much raw capability you bring to a roll, but they do not determine your Stones.

  • Stones Define Affinity
    Stones are gained through Lifetime Experience and may be assigned to Attributes or converted into Permanent Colorless Stones. They replace class features with a modular supernatural toolkit, independent of how high or low the linked Attribute is. You decide where your supernatural affinity develops and what kind of hero you become.

  • Raises Create Drama
    You may always meet the Target Number for a normal success, but by risking more, by raising the stakes, you unlock special effects, crushing blows, and cinematic moments. Each Raise is a gamble and a story beat.

  • Actions and Reactions Matter
    Every round is a choice: attack, defend, maneuver, or risk everything. Reactions keep you engaged even when it’s not your turn — parries, dodges, counterstrikes, and warnings make combat feel alive.

  • Simple Dice, Big Moments
    Rolls explode. Success is clear. The math is fast, but the outcomes are cinematic. You will know when you land a decisive strike — and when fate turns against you.

The Mastery System is built for fast, tactical, and narrative-rich play. It is a game where numbers represent potential, but choices define outcomes. You are not just rolling dice, you are gambling with destiny, bending your assigned Stones to fuel extraordinary feats, and carving your legend into the world. In Mastery, every success feels earned, and every failure pushes the story forward. It is a system that rewards boldness, creativity, and mastery itself.

The Role of the Players

You begin as scattered survivors remnants of a fallen world, bound by fading memories and a spark of defiance. The game assumes you are not for the demons and that you would join if possible the last embers of rebellion struggling against the demonic order. Whether you fight for freedom, redemption, or your own survival, your story begins in the ashes of the old world.

This is a sandbox, not a railroad. No one will hand you missions or tell you what to do. You decide where to go, who to trust, and what risks to take. The GM shapes the world’s response, but you set the course every decision carries weight.

The world of Destroyed Faith is harsh and uncertain. Resources are scarce, allies are fragile, and every act of mercy or defiance matters. Killing a marked host destroys the vessel but not the demon, saving one may cost lives but can inspire hope in others. Your victories will be small, your sacrifices great yet even the smallest triumph proves that the darkness can bleed.

“Hope is not given, it is made.”
— Teachings of the Hidden Flame

Characters are defined by seven attributes. Each point in an attribute grants 1 die to the related Pool, but attributes in the Mastery System are not statistics, they are channels of inner power. Your attributes represent how deeply you can reach into the divine spark within you, your capacity to focus, release, and shape the energy of your own soul.

At character creation, no Attribute may exceed 4 and no starting Attribute is lower than 2. Attributes determine the size of your dice Pools. They do not generate Stones. Stones are gained through Lifetime Experience and are assigned independently to Attribute affinities or converted into Permanent Colorless Stones. Later progression can push Attributes beyond 4, where raw capability grows increasingly exceptional.

The Seven Attributes

Attribute Concept Expression
Might Strength and presence of the body How fully you can turn your will into force and motion.
Agility Reflex, balance, and flow How purely you move with instinct and momentum.
Vitality Endurance and survival How strongly your body can hold the spark of life.
Intellect Knowledge and arcane structure How far your mind can reach into the patterns of creation.
Resolve Willpower and inner stability How fiercely your soul resists corruption and bends reality instead of breaking.
Influence Charisma and presence How brightly your essence resonates with others and commands the world through emotion.
Wits Awareness and reaction How swiftly your consciousness adapts and shapes events before they unfold.

::

Every hero begins with seven core attributes:
Might, Agility, Vitality, Intellect, Resolve, Influence, and Wits.

At character creation, attributes no longer use a free point-buy pool. Instead, assign the following fixed values across your seven attributes:

  • 2 attributes at 4
  • 2 attributes at 3
  • 3 attributes at 2

Each value may be assigned freely, but no Attribute may exceed 4 or begin below 2 at creation.

Example Attribute Spreads

The following examples show how the starting values 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 might be assigned to different character concepts. These are not classes or fixed builds. They only show how Attribute choices shape your early dice Pools and combat direction. Starting Stone assignment is a separate build choice.

Frontline Fighter

Might 4, Vitality 4, Agility 3, Wits 3, Resolve 2, Influence 2, Intellect 2

This player assigns the two starting Stones to Might and Vitality. That assignment is a build choice, not a consequence of the Attribute values. They are built to hit hard, survive pressure, and hold the front line.

Mobile Skirmisher

Agility 4, Wits 4, Might 3, Vitality 3, Resolve 2, Influence 2, Intellect 2

This player assigns the two starting Stones to Agility and Wits. The same Attributes could have received different Stones if the player wanted a different supernatural focus. They rely on speed, positioning, reactions, and tempo rather than standing still and trading blows.

Spellcaster

Intellect 4, Resolve 4, Vitality 3, Wits 3, Influence 2, Agility 2, Might 2

This player assigns the two starting Stones to Intellect and Resolve. Attribute placement and Stone placement remain separate choices. They are built around spell pressure, resistance, rituals, and Stone options that support casting.

Example: Alaris Chooses Her Attributes

Alaris is built as a mobile melee skirmisher. She chooses her Elorian Echo first, as required by the Character Creation steps. The examples in this book are grouped by topic for easier reference, rather than presented in the chronological order of her decisions. She survives through movement, Evade, and Phasing rather than heavy armor, so her highest Attribute values support that identity.

Attribute Value Why Alaris chooses it
Agility 4 Her primary combat Attribute. It supports Finesse attacks, Evade, and movement-based Professions.
Vitality 4 Gives her enough Health to remain in melee when an attack does connect.
Might 3 Keeps her dangerous with a greatsword and supports physical actions.
Wits 3 Supports awareness, tracking, and fast battlefield decisions.
Resolve 2 Gives her basic inner stability and supports several social and occult approaches.
Influence 2 Lets her participate meaningfully in social scenes.
Intellect 2 Structured analysis and academic spellcasting are not central to this concept.

Alaris then assigns her two starting Stones independently: one Agility Stone and one Vitality Stone. Echo Imprints (next step): Both Agility and Vitality are 4, so Alaris may select Imprints from either Attribute. At starting MR 2, she chooses Catfall (Agility) and Living Warmth (Vitality) as her two free Echo Imprints. Their supernatural effects and Echo Memories do not replace Movement or Healing Powers.

What this example shows

Start with the character's intended playstyle, then place the fixed values where they support that playstyle. The lowest Attribute is not a punishment; it identifies what the character is not trying to specialize in.

Professions and Training

"Your past tells us what you might know. Your method tells us which Attribute you use."

A Profession describes work, training, or a formative period of life: Burglar, Tracker, Woodcutter, Juggler, Courtier, Former Prisoner, or any comparably grounded concept. It covers practical knowledge, contacts, habits, and techniques credibly learned from that experience. Professions replace lists of narrow player Skills. Every character chooses four Professions at Rank 2 during creation and receives Perception Rank 2 separately for free.

A player describes their method and explains how a Profession helps. The GM decides whether that link is credible and selects a relevant Attribute; professions never prescribe fixed Attributes. A broad title must have an agreed concrete scope: Assassin - worked as a quiet contract killer in Karaveth is useful; Good at Everything is not.

No automatic permissions: Professions do not grant Powers, Spell access, weapon attacks, combat bonuses, Stone Abilities, extra Actions, or the ability to perform impossible tasks. Someone with no suitable Profession may still try an ordinary feasible task as untrained. Only a task that truly requires particular knowledge, tools, or access may be unavailable without a credible alternative method.

One Training Roll, Two Comparisons

Training Roll = Relevant Attribute k Mastery Rank, with Training Advantage and optional Training Crit.

Roll the normal exploding d8 Pool, applying equipment, Health, Fear, and other valid modifiers. Training Rank improves only how the existing dice behave; it never adds dice or changes Keep. This procedure is used for a relevant Profession or for the separately trained Perception ability.

Check Resolution Raises
Standard Training Check Compare the result against a GM-set Task TN. Meet or exceed it. Optional Raises, declared before rolling, add +4 TN each.
Comparative Training Check Each side rolls once with its own Attribute, MR, applicable Profession or Perception Rank, and modifiers. Higher result wins. No Raises and no additional Task TN.

Choose Standard if no capable active opponent contests the task. Choose Comparative if one creature actively counters another (for instance, a Burglar's quiet approach versus a guard's Perception, a Courtier's deception versus an investigator's scrutiny, or a Tracker obscuring signs versus a pursuer reading them). Ties favor the observing or defending party; otherwise the status quo remains. When no professional/trained method applies and the contest is an immediate clash of raw capacity, use the separate Opposed Attribute Contest rules.

Training Rank Progression

Rank Training Training Advantage Training Crit (per Tyhran Day)
0 Untrained Disadvantage; no Training Advantage -
1 Novice May reroll initial 1s -
2 Apprentice May reroll initial 1s-2s -
3 Trained May reroll initial 1s-3s -
4 Professional May reroll initial 1s-4s -
5 Expert May reroll initial 1s-5s -
6 Master May reroll initial 1s-6s -
7 Grandmaster May reroll initial 1s-6s 1 use
8 Legendary May reroll initial 1s-6s 2 uses

Training Advantage: On a Training Roll using one relevant learned Profession, or Perception, you may reroll any or all initial Pool dice within the Rank's listed range. Each die can be rerolled only once, and the new result must be kept. Apply Training Advantage before resolving natural explosions and Keep; explosion-only dice cannot be rerolled by Training Advantage. Other ordinary Advantage sources do not permit a second reroll of a die already rerolled this way. Natural 8s explode normally.

Training Crit: At Rank 7 or higher, designate a Training Roll using that learned Profession or Perception for Critical before rolling. Natural 7s and 8s explode on that roll, including qualifying explosions. Rank 7 provides one use and Rank 8 two uses per Tyhran Day per Profession or Perception; no carry-over. Training Crit modifies the Training Roll, not Damage Dice, and cannot stack with another Critical source on the same roll. Separately imposed Disadvantage still limits eligible exploding dice. In a Comparative Training Check, both sides declare Training Crit before either result is revealed.

Untrained: If no Profession or Perception applies, roll full Attribute k MR with Disadvantage (only one eligible die may explode), no Training Advantage, no Training Crit, and no Raises. Untrained attempts are not prohibited merely for lacking a named occupation.

Beta Profession Respec (Optional)

A GM may enable the World Setting Allow Profession Respec (Beta). While it is on, a player may freely replace or edit one of their four free starting Professions — choosing another catalogue Profession or a custom Profession, and editing name, origin/background, description/scope, and category — while keeping the existing Rank and invested XP. Example: Burglar Rank 5 becomes Blacksmith Rank 5 at no XP cost. Perception is never changed. Disabling the setting blocks free replacement but does not block normal XP advancement. Existing characters and legacy migrations remain safe; the four starting slots are preserved without duplicating records.

Profession Examples (Approved Catalogue)

The following ninety examples are suggestions only — never a whitelist. Characters may always invent a custom Profession with an agreed scope.

Trades

Professions are lived experience, not a closed skill list. Choose four at Rank 2, plus Perception at Rank 2 for free.

Blacksmith:
You can forge and repair iron tools, judge the quality of metalwork, and recognize the marks left by faulty tools or unusual workshop methods.

Armorer:
You understand how armor is made, fitted, maintained, and repaired, and can recognize weak joints, damaged plates, or an unfamiliar style of protection.

Carpenter:
You can build or repair wooden structures, assess doors and beams, and spot construction details that might hide an opening or reveal an unsafe building.

Locksmith:
You understand locks, keys, and their mechanisms, and can examine a damaged lock, repair its parts, or explain how a particular design might be opened.

Tanner:
You know how hides are prepared and preserved, can identify leatherworking materials, and recognize the smells and residues of a tannery.

Tailor:
You can cut, fit, and mend clothing, recognize expensive or unusual fabrics, and use the details of a garment to infer its origin or purpose.

Glassblower:
You know how glass is shaped and cooled, can judge vessels and lenses, and recognize fractures or flaws that may make a glass object dangerous.

Mason:
You understand stone construction, mortar, and load-bearing walls, and can identify weak joints, recent repairs, or passages concealed within masonry.

Potter:
You can shape and fire clay vessels, recognize common glazes and kilns, and notice when a container has been resealed or made for a special purpose.

Apothecary:
You know how to prepare and store remedies, handle ingredients, and recognize common preparations, although identifying rare substances may require further investigation.

Baker:
You know ovens, grains, and food preparation, and can recognize spoiled ingredients, manage a busy bakehouse, or find practical work in an unfamiliar settlement.

Brewer:
You understand fermentation, brewing vessels, and cellar work, and can judge whether a drink has spoiled, been watered down, or been tampered with.

Innkeeper:
You know hospitality, supplies, guests, and local gossip, and can judge a traveler's needs or recognize the ordinary routines of a roadside inn.

Merchant:
You can value familiar goods, negotiate prices, read market behavior, and recognize when a deal, shipment, or contract seems unusually risky.

Market Broker:
You know how buyers and sellers find one another, can assess market demand, and recognize the customs and middlemen behind local trade.

Shipwright:
You understand hulls, ribs, rigging supports, and ship repairs, and can assess whether a vessel is seaworthy or has been recently altered.

Bloodsilver Assayer:
You recognize the methods used to examine Bloodsilver, can inspect marks and measurements, and know which traders or officials normally verify its authenticity.

Kalgrad Forge Tender:
You know the routines of Kalgrad forges, including fuel, tools, and furnace care, and can recognize interruptions or irregularities in forge operations.

Wilderness

The wilderness rewards familiarity with terrain, weather, beasts, and the rhythms of travel.

Woodcutter:
You can fell and split timber safely, read the condition of trees, and find practical routes through working forests and logging grounds.

Tracker:
You can interpret footprints, broken vegetation, and disturbed earth to estimate where a creature went and how recently it passed.

Wilderness Scout:
You know how to travel quietly, observe camps from cover, recognize field signs, and return with useful information about difficult ground.

Forest Guide:
You understand woodland landmarks, seasonal trails, and local dangers, and can lead travelers around obstacles without relying on a marked road.

Trapper:
You can set and examine snares, recognize animal habits, and determine whether a trap was disturbed by prey, weather, or another person.

Hunter:
You know how to stalk game, judge tracks and wind direction, and prepare what you catch without wasting useful resources.

Herbalist:
You can identify familiar wild plants, gather them without ruining the source, and recognize those that are useful, harmful, or easily confused.

Falconer:
You understand the care and training of birds of prey, can read their behavior, and recognize the equipment used by professional handlers.

Beast Handler:
You can safely restrain and transport difficult animals, read warning signs, and improvise practical ways to calm a frightened creature.

Marsh Guide:
You know how to find firm ground among reeds and pools, recognize dangerous water, and follow routes that disappear with the seasons.

Desert Guide:
You can estimate travel needs in arid country, recognize useful landmarks, and judge how heat, sand, or scarce water will affect a journey.

Pathfinder:
You can select a route through unknown terrain, weigh distance against danger, and recognize signs that a path has recently been used.

River Forager:
You know riverbanks, reeds, and shallow waters, and can find food or materials while noticing changes in currents and seasonal flooding.

Cave Explorer:
You understand cave passages, rope work, and underground hazards, and can recognize unstable ground or signs of earlier visitors.

Ruin Explorer:
You know how to move through damaged structures, identify unsafe surfaces, and distinguish old collapse from signs of recent entry.

Storm Watcher:
You can read clouds, winds, and changing pressure, and recognize weather patterns that may threaten travel, camps, or exposed settlements.

Caravan Master:
You can organize supplies and animals for a long journey, judge delays, and identify practical risks along trade routes.

Astralan Mist Runner:
You know how Astralan routes change in the mist, can follow subtle landmarks, and recognize the hazards of moving where visibility fails.

Society

A city's doors open through reputation, persuasion, cunning, or an understanding of its hidden routines.

Burglar:
You understand doors, windows, alarms, and escape routes, and can plan a quiet entry or recognize the weak points of a guarded building.

Cat Burglar:
You are practiced at approaching buildings by roofs, ledges, and upper windows, and can judge handholds and unnoticed routes above street level.

Pickpocket:
You understand crowded movement, distracting gestures, and the placement of valuables, and can recognize when someone is working a crowd.

Forger:
You know seals, signatures, and document materials, and can imitate familiar records or spot inconsistencies in suspicious paperwork.

Smuggler:
You understand hidden cargo, bribery, false declarations, and unofficial routes, and can recognize how goods move beyond ordinary inspection.

Spy:
You know how to observe without drawing attention, maintain a cover story, and gather information from contacts while protecting your identity.

Informant:
You understand the trade in rumors and secrets, and can judge whom to approach, what a source wants, and whether information sounds planted.

Disguise Artist:
You can alter clothing, posture, and presentation, and know which small details make an assumed identity believable to a casual observer.

Juggler:
You have practiced precise hand movements, public performances, and timed distractions, and can use those skills when a situation rewards coordination.

Courtier:
You know etiquette, favors, titles, and the unspoken rules of court, and can judge how to approach someone without causing offense.

Herald:
You know coats of arms, formal announcements, and noble lineages, and can recognize ceremonial errors or a claim of questionable status.

Political Organizer:
You understand meetings, factions, public sentiment, and recruitment, and can build support or recognize who influences a community.

Street Urchin:
You grew up navigating alleys, shelters, and informal street networks, and know how to find food, information, or a place to hide.

Beggar:
You understand shelters, charitable habits, and the flow of street life, and may notice details ignored by people who rarely look down.

Refugee:
You know how to adapt without secure possessions or status, locate practical aid, and understand the pressures within displaced communities.

Servant:
You understand household routines, deliveries, back entrances, and etiquette, and can recognize when a residence is running differently than usual.

Hidden Flame Courier:
You understand discreet deliveries, safe houses, and resistance contacts, and know why secrecy and trustworthy routes matter to the Hidden Flame.

Demon House Steward:
You know the hierarchy and daily routines of a Demon House, and can interpret records, servants' behavior, and changes in household procedure.

Conflict

These backgrounds represent experience around violence, military structures, and security.

City Watchman:
You know patrol routines, local enforcement procedures, and public disturbances, and can recognize when guards or criminals depart from expected behavior.

Sentry:
You understand watch rotations, fields of view, and alarm procedures, and can judge where an entrance or camp is most vulnerable.

Patrol Scout:
You are accustomed to moving ahead of armed groups, reading recent traces, and reporting dangers without exposing the main force.

Mercenary:
You understand paid campaigns, contract obligations, and rough deployments, and know how professional fighting companies recruit and operate.

Militia Member:
You know local defense drills, musters, and improvised preparations, and can help organize civilians when a settlement faces danger.

Bodyguard:
You are trained to notice threats to a protected person, assess exits and crowds, and plan safer movement through hostile surroundings.

Captain:
You understand command structures, orders, and morale, and can coordinate personnel or recognize when a unit is close to breaking down.

Quartermaster:
You understand supplies, rations, equipment records, and shortages, and can recognize unusual requisitions or prepare a force for a demanding march.

Gate Guard:
You understand inspections, access records, and common pretexts for entry, and can recognize when a visitor or delivery warrants closer scrutiny.

Prison Jailer:
You know locks, watch routines, inmate behavior, and secure transfers, and can judge how confinement procedures might be compromised.

Field Medic:
You are practiced at triage, bandaging, casualty transport, and care under pressure, allowing you to apply the existing medical rules where appropriate.

Siege Engineer:
You understand fortifications, siege machines, and approaches to defended positions, and can identify structural weaknesses or practical obstacles.

Military Engineer:
You know bridges, earthworks, field defenses, and logistics, and can assess how terrain or damaged infrastructure affects a campaign.

Naval Marine:
You are accustomed to shipboard security, boarding routines, and cramped fighting environments, and understand the hazards of armed service at sea.

Interrogator:
You know interviewing methods, pressure tactics, and inconsistent testimony, and can recognize when a subject is withholding information.

Bounty Hunter:
You understand warrants, informants, and pursuit routines, and can trace a target through contacts, records, or practical signs of travel.

Sentinel Signal Keeper:
You understand traditional Sentinel commands, warning signs, and patrol signals, and can recognize when a message or procedure seems incorrect.

Hidden Flame Quartermaster:
You know how the Hidden Flame hides, distributes, and records supplies, and can recognize the logistical needs of a clandestine cell.

Knowledge

Knowledge comes from study, observation, and repeated practice.

Physician:
You understand symptoms, diagnosis, and traditional treatment, and can evaluate a patient and apply the existing rules for medical care.

Surgeon:
You know anatomy, surgical tools, and wound treatment, and can recognize injuries or procedures that require specialist attention.

Herbal Physician:
You understand medicinal plants and their preparation, and can recognize common remedies, dangerous mixtures, or mistakes in dosage.

Anatomist:
You have studied the structure of living bodies, and can interpret unusual wounds or identify anatomical details others might overlook.

Detective:
You know investigative routines, records, and interviews, and can connect scattered clues without assuming that every witness is reliable.

Forensic Examiner:
You can inspect physical evidence, marks, and remains, and recognize details that suggest how or when an event occurred.

Scholar:
You know how to consult sources, question claims, and organize research, and can identify which field of knowledge may hold an answer.

Historian:
You understand chronicles, dates, and competing accounts, and can recognize anachronisms or trace a claim to its earliest known source.

Archivist:
You know how records are classified, stored, and altered, and can retrieve obscure information or notice gaps in an official archive.

Linguist:
You understand how languages change and relate, and can analyze unfamiliar grammar, names, or inscriptions without automatically knowing their meaning.

Cartographer:
You know how to draw and interpret maps, compare distances, and recognize when a chart is inaccurate, incomplete, or deliberately misleading.

Architect:
You understand plans, building styles, and structural design, and can assess the intended function or weaknesses of a constructed space.

Astronomer:
You can track celestial movements and calculate observations, and recognize irregularities in calendars, star charts, or recorded night skies.

Theologian:
You know religious doctrines, debates, and histories, and can distinguish established teachings from local interpretations or deliberate heresy.

Ritual Assistant:
You understand the preparation, tools, and formal steps of rites you have witnessed, but your background alone does not grant magical powers.

Omen Interpreter:
You know customary signs, prophecies, and divination traditions, and can explain what an omen would mean to a particular community.

Velenor Star Reader:
You know Velenor traditions of observing the skies, and can interpret familiar charts and the cultural importance of celestial events.

Red Priest Scribe:
You know the records, formulas, and terminology used by Red Priest scribes, and can recognize suspicious alterations to familiar documents.

Standard Training Checks and Raises

  1. Describe the task: The player explains the intended outcome and method. The GM chooses a fitting Attribute, the relevant Profession (if any), and the Base TN = Task Level x 4 based on the task, not the actor's MR.
  2. Declare Raises (optional): The player declares additional feasible effects before rolling. Each Raise increases the Task TN by +4. Profession Rank grants no Free Raises, and there is no Rank-based Raise allowance or cap.
  3. Roll: Use Attribute k MR with any applicable Training Advantage and declared Training Crit. Meet or exceed Final TN = Base TN + (4 x declared Raises).
  4. Resolve: On success, apply the basic outcome plus exactly the declared feasible additional effects. On failure, none of those effects is achieved. A high roll never grants undeclared Raises.
Task Level Difficulty Base TN Example
1 Simple 4 Hammer a nail into prepared wood
2 Easy 8 Forge ordinary nails; follow obvious tracks
3 Moderate 12 Repair an ordinary tool
4 Demanding 16 Forge a reliable sword; treat illness under pressure
5 Difficult 20 Diagnose a complex illness quickly
6 Very difficult 24 Forge an unusual alloy blade
7 Exceptional 28 Solve a rare professional problem
8+ Extraordinary 32+ Accomplish an unprecedented feat

Raise effects (one Raise each)

Effect Benefit
Scope Double similar eligible units or coverage (2 Raises = x4; 3 = x8)
Speed Halve feasible work time (2 Raises = one quarter)
Quality Improve workmanship, durability, clarity, or persuasiveness by one suitable step
Efficiency Reduce avoidable waste or effort by one practical step
Insight Gain one additional fact, inference, or clue supported by the evidence
Safety Prevent or reduce one foreseeable secondary complication

Raises improve an outcome already possible with the character's method, tools, and circumstances. They create no supernatural ability, free attack, or guaranteed control. Comparative Training Checks never use Raises. Combat and Ritual Raises retain their separate rules.

Defining and Advancing Professions

Write each Profession as: a concrete name, where or how it was learned, and a one-sentence agreed scope. "Woodcutter (Kalgrad forest camps) - trees, axes as work tools, timber hauling, and mountain trails" is a Profession. "Everything Outdoors" is too broad. A player may propose any credible profession or formative life background; an example catalogue is inspirational, not a closed selection list.

One Profession per check. When more than one of your Professions could apply, use one fitting Rank, never add Ranks or combine rerolls. The player may propose an unexpected application, explain their history, and let the GM judge it. An actor can try a possible task without relevant training using the untrained rule. The GM should not arbitrarily increase the TN merely because the selected background has a different title than an expected narrow skill; genuine differences in method, risk, or circumstances may affect the task's difficulty.

Non-combat boundary: Professions never replace a weapon's Attack Pool, an Attack roll, a Spell Casting roll, a Power, or a Combat Sense. They can plausibly support preparation, specialized knowledge, climbing, concealment, investigation, social leverage, or other noncombat tasks. A purported 'Assassin' must define which kinds of professional experience they possess; it does not make every combat roll trained.

Routine work: A trained character can complete familiar work within the competence of their Profession when appropriate tools, time, and conditions are available. This grants only the basic outcome, never undeclared Raise effects. Passive Training Value = 2 x relevant Attribute may settle calm eligible Standard Training Checks, even with predeclared Raises, if it meets the Final TN. It never applies to Comparative Checks, urgent danger, or instability; Training Advantage and Training Crit require a roll.

Perception: Every character separately receives Perception Rank 2 for free; it is not a Profession slot. Perception follows the same Rank 0-8, Training Advantage, Training Crit, and XP progression. It is used to detect present movement, sound, concealment, creatures, and other sensory information. A relevant Profession may interpret evidence (Tracker reads old footprints, Investigator reconstructs a scene) but does not replace or stack with Perception when the task is simply detecting a present target. A Special Combat Sense determines what can be sensed, not whether perception succeeds.

Attribute Typical Perception method
Wits Movement, sound, hidden presence, and ambush cues
Intellect Visible anomalies, spatial clues, and technical inconsistencies
Resolve Occult/spiritual pressure, if a valid active Sense supports it

Creation: Choose four distinct Professions at Rank 2, plus free Perception Rank 2. There is no separate creation-point pool. Advancement: A new Rank 1 Profession costs 4 XP. Rank 2 also costs 4 XP; each later Rank costs 2 XP more than the preceding one. The costs for Ranks 1-8 are 4 / 4 / 6 / 8 / 10 / 12 / 14 / 16 XP, including Perception. Going from Rank 0 to 8 costs 74 XP; advancing an initial Rank 2 Profession to Rank 8 costs 66 XP. Consecutive ranks require the full cost of intermediate steps. Learning a new Profession or broadening an existing one's agreed scope needs credible events or training in the story; expanding the scope does not happen automatically from Rank increases.

Armor and Shields: Printed Physical Training dice penalties instead apply to physical Profession attempts, and to other physically impeded trained tasks, whichever Attribute is chosen. These penalties do not change the normal Combat Pools.

Worked Examples

  1. Blacksmith 4 - Standard: Craft ordinary nails at Base TN 8. Declare two Scope Raises (Final TN 16) for four batches. Use Training Advantage to reroll initial 1s-4s.
  2. Field Medic 4 - Standard: With Intellect 4, MR 2, treat illness at TN 16. Declare one Safety Raise (Final TN 20). Roll 4k2 with Training Advantage.
  3. Burglar vs. Perception - Comparative: A trained Burglar achieves 24 while a guard gets 21 on Perception. The Burglar's concealed approach succeeds; no other Task TN or Raises apply.
  4. Forensic Examiner 5 - Standard: Investigate a disturbed room at TN 16 with two Insight Raises (Final TN 24), potentially revealing two more supported clues.
  5. Untrained healing: Anyone may clean a superficial wound with an appropriate Attribute and Disadvantage; complex surgery requires actual expertise and tools.
  6. Alaris at creation: Choose Wilderness Scout 2, Caravan Master 2, Field Medic 2, and Street Urchin 2, plus Perception 2 for free. Each is a part of her history, not an entry in a narrow fixed skill list.
  7. Invisible movement: A player describes how their Burglar or Juggler training lets them move quietly. Roll that fitting Profession against observing guards' Perception. If Invisibility covers the guard's Sense, apply the higher of the Profession result and Invisibility TN, never their sum. No fixed movement-distance limit exists.

Example catalogue: See the separate Destroyed Faith - Profession Inspiration Catalogue. The professions and categories listed there are optional ideas; players and GMs may create their own.

Group Ambush — Coordinated Stealth

A group may attempt one coordinated Comparative concealment Check to approach or occupy plausible ambush positions without being detected. The designated specialist uses a fitting Profession (such as Burglar, Wilderness Scout, or Assassin with an appropriate scope) or the untrained rules; all observers use Perception. There are no Raises, separate setup TN, bonus attacks, or extra combat Rounds.

  1. Select the specialist. The group chooses a participating character with the highest fitting Profession Rank for the declared approach. If several tie, the group chooses one. The specialist uses their own relevant Attribute k MR, Training Advantage, and any declared Training Crit; if none has a relevant Profession, the attempt is untrained.
  2. Include every participant's equipment penalty. Add together all Physical Training dice penalties from armor and equipped shields worn by every participating ambusher, including the specialist. Subtract that total from the specialist's Attribute Pool before rolling, using the normal two-rolled-dice floor on legal standard rolls. Medium Armor: -1d8; Heavy Armor: -2d8; Parry Shield: -1d8; Medium/Tower Shield: -2d8. Light Armor has no such penalty. Do not add the other characters' Attributes or Training Ranks to the Pool.
  3. Roll once for the group. Apply the specialist's Training Advantage and optional Training Crit to the reduced Pool. The result represents coordinated concealment for every eligible participant. Members do not make additional individual rolls or contribute Raises. The group needs a credible method, route, cover, and opportunity; even a high Profession Rank cannot conceal an impossible position.
  4. Oppose with Perception. Every observer with a plausible detection cue may make one Perception Training Roll using their own Attribute, MR, Training Advantage, and optional Training Crit. Compare it directly to the group's concealment result; a tie favors the observer. Detection remains observer-specific; warnings travel only as the fiction permits.
  5. Resolve Surprise normally. When combat begins, participating ambushers gain Surprise Priority only against enemies who remain unaware of them, following the existing Surprise rule. Roll Initiative and Initiative Exchange normally. Surprise Priority applies during the first Round only and grants no extra turn or automatic damage bonus.

Example: A specialist has 12d8. Three group members wear Heavy Armor (-6d8) and one Medium Armor (-1d8), so the group rolls 5k3 at MR 3. If the specialist has Burglar 6 with a fitting concealment scope, reroll initial 1s-6s through Training Advantage. Training Crit is unavailable below Rank 7. Compare the result to each eligible guard's Perception roll.

Limits: Only characters actually following the same feasible coordinated plan are covered. Characters taking an independent route or revealing themselves require separate resolution. A group ambush roll covers the agreed approach and coherent, careful movement along that plan. There is no fixed distance limit on Stealth. Overt hostile actions or abandoning the agreed concealment can end ordinary Stealth; a material change of circumstances may require a new attempt. Do not demand repeated rolls merely for continued movement or against unchanged opposition.

Related systems: Ordinary concealment attempts and Invisibility remain separate. Invisibility retains its own sense-specific TN. Opposed Attribute Contests are Attribute-only and use no Profession training. Summons use eligible natural abilities with the owner's Profession Training Rolls; Rituals retain their distinct Sealed-Stone costs and effect tiers.

Choose your Powers

Powers are the abilities that define how your character acts in play.

They are not classes.
They are not fixed builds. They are not prescribed roles. A character chooses Powers to define what they can do in combat, how they survive, how they move, how they react, and how they express their mastery.

Starting Powers

At character creation, choose two Active Powers at Power Level 2. In addition, choose a number of Passives equal to your available Passive Slots, plus one Reaction and one Active Buff Power at Power Level 4. Characters normally begin at MR 2 and therefore choose two Passives. If the campaign begins at MR 1, choose one Passive instead. Starting exception: the granted Passive, Reaction, and Active Buff remain at PL 4 at MR 1. The normal PL 2 cap applies to other Powers and subsequent purchases/upgrades.

Power Level

Each Power has a Power Level (PL). A Power's Power Level determines which level of that Power you use. If a Power is Power Level 1, use its Power Level 1 entry. If a Power is Power Level 2, use its Power Level 2 entry. Power Level is the only progression value needed for Powers. Do not create a separate Spell Level, Tree Level, Class Level, or similar value.

Power Types & Catalogues

Every Power belongs to one Power Type. Each Power Type follows its own rules, templates, limits, and examples. The Core Rulebook only explains the general role of Powers. The external Power Catalogues are the rules source for building, reading, and resolving specific Powers.

Use the Power Catalogues when you need to know:

  • how a Power is built,
  • which templates are available,
  • how Power Points are priced,
  • what each Power Level grants,
  • how examples are resolved,
  • how Areas of Effect, Autofire, Split-Attack, and other multi-target techniques work,
  • how Powers interact with Armor, Evade, Specials, Damage Reduction, movement, and action economy.
Power Type / Catalogue Use it for
Actives Action-based Powers: attacks, Scarred-Bar Restoration, Cleanse, Specials, AoE, Autofire, Split-Attack, zones, barriers, and other direct effects.
Passives Always-on or pre-selected character features: Armor, Evade, Damage, Health, Damage Reduction, Phasing, and passive Special support.
Active Buffs Temporary combat states: stances, auras, offensive/defensive boosts, and maintained effects. Size-changing Transformations use their own noncombat rules; visual Form does not change mechanics.
Reactions Immediate answers to specific triggers: defenses, counters, emergency protection, interception, and trigger-based responses.
Movement Powers Movement replacements: dash, leap, teleport, flight, burrow, wall movement, phase passage, and similar movement options.
Mentalist Option

A character may build around Mental Powers by choosing Telepathy as a Passive. Telepathy grants Telepathic Access and includes voluntary Mind Links at no additional Power cost. The character may then choose Mental Attack, Mind Illusion, Mind Probe, or Mental Control as Active Powers. A Mental Power's Power Level cannot normally exceed the character's Passive: Telepathy Power Level.

Spells

A Spell is not a separate Power type. Spell is a delivery method for an eligible Ranged Active Power. The underlying Power keeps its Power Level, Range, Damage, AoE, Duration, Specials, action type, and base Technical Reference. Spell delivery changes how the Power is rolled and resisted. A Ranged Active with Specials may use Spell delivery normally. A character may also have a number of Special-less Spell Powers equal to Mastery Rank. A Spell uses Intellect, Resolve, or Influence as its fixed casting source. See the Magic rules for Casting Rolls, Spell TN, Spell Resistance, and the full Special-less Spell limit.

Building a Character

When choosing Powers, think about what your character actually does during play.

A complete character usually wants some mix of:

  • a way to affect enemies,
  • a way to survive pressure,
  • a way to move or control position,
  • and a way to respond when threatened.

You do not need to cover every category. A fragile sniper, a fortress guardian, a battlefield controller, and a mobile duelist may all choose very different Power mixes. What matters is that each Power has a clear job. For examples, templates, and detailed build guidance, use the external Power Catalogue documents.

Example: Alaris Chooses Her Powers

Alaris begins at MR 2 and uses the standard starting package: two Actives at Power Level 2, plus two Passives, one Active Buff, and one Reaction at Power Level 4.

Power Power Level Role in the build
Melee Single Target Attack 2 Reliable direct weapon damage.
Melee Single Target Special: Sundered 2 Applies Sundered to prepare the target for later non-Spell attacks. This Special-only Power deals no direct Attack Damage: no Power, Weapon or Spell Focus Damage, and no Damage Roll.
Passive: Evade 4 Raises her everyday defense against direct attacks.
Passive: Phasing 4 Establishes Phasing at the start of combat.
Active Buff: Phasing 4 Reinforces that Phasing defense during difficult fights.
Reaction: Phasing 4 Provides an immediate answer to a decisive hit.

The two Actives give Alaris a choice between immediate damage and preparing a target for the group. Her defensive Powers then commit to one clear identity: Evade handles ordinary pressure, while Phasing protects her from the hits that matter most.

Choose a Language

All souls share the Common Tongue, born from the Echoes of the First War.
Every character also learns one additional language. For some Echoes, this language is fixed by their origin and cannot be chosen freely.

  • Dwarves automatically learn Dwarvish.
  • Dragonborn automatically learn Draconic.
  • Sentinels automatically learn Mustelic.
  • Elorians automatically learn Elvish.
  • Characters of all other Echoes choose their additional language freely to reflect their origin, training, culture, or story.

::

Languages of the Known Realms

  • Common Tongue – spoken by all civilized nations
  • Arcane – language of runes, sigils, and scholars of the old world
  • Infernal – the whispered bargains of hell
  • Celestial – hymns of the divine and long-fallen angels
  • Dwarvish – forged words of stone and steel
  • The First – ancient tongue of the Titan-born
  • Elvish – fluid and timeless, carried by wind and memory
  • Draconic – the primal roar of flame, wave, and storm
  • Mustelic – the precise command-tongue of Sentinels and divine law

Example

A Human with a demonic mark might choose Infernal. Their languages are: Common Tongue, Infernal. An Elorian wanderer automatically learns Elvish. Their languages are: Common Tongue, Elvish.

“Power leaves traces — in the body, in the soul, and in the world around you.”

Schticks are narrative signatures created by the power awakening within a character. They may be physical, visual, audible, emotional, or supernatural: an unnatural eye color, frost gathering on the skin, a voice that carries a strange echo, sparks appearing during moments of anger, or shadows briefly moving against the light. Schticks show how Mastery changes a character. They make growing power visible in the fiction, but they are not Powers, abilities, or mechanical upgrades.

What Are Schticks?

A Schtick is a distinctive trait that makes a character recognizable and shows how their inner power manifests in the world. Schticks have no mechanical effect. They do not change Attributes, Professions, dice pools, Target Numbers, Damage, Armor, Evade, Movement, Senses, concealment, social rolls, or any other game value. A Schtick may influence how the world is described or how NPCs react in the fiction, but it never grants an automatic bonus, penalty, success, failure, or special capability.

A Schtick describes what your power looks or feels like. It does not determine what your power can do.

If a trait should provide an actual mechanical effect, it must come from a Power, Echo, Artifact, Stone Ability, or another rule that explicitly grants that effect.

Acquisition

You gain one Schtick for each Mastery Rank you possess.

A character therefore has:

Mastery Rank Schticks
MR 1 1
MR 2 2
MR 3 3
MR 4 4
MR 5 5
MR 6 6
MR 7 7
MR 8 8

A character beginning at MR 2 therefore starts with two Schticks. When your Mastery Rank increases, choose another Schtick that represents how your growing power has changed you. Schticks are normally permanent. They may change through major transformations, rituals, Artifact awakenings, Echo developments, or other significant events if the player and GM agree that the change fits the story.

Progressive Manifestation

Schticks generally become more striking as Mastery increases. Early manifestations are subtle enough to be dismissed as unusual. At higher Mastery, the character may visibly appear touched by forces beyond ordinary mortal nature.

The following scale is a guideline for tone rather than a mechanical restriction:

Mastery Rank Manifestation Scale Example — Frost
MR 1 — Minor Trait A subtle physical or sensory peculiarity. Your breath mists even in warm rooms.
MR 2 — Distinct Feature A clearly unusual characteristic others may notice. Your touch feels cold and moisture briefly crystallizes against your skin.
MR 3 — Defining Aspect Your power visibly marks your body or presence. Pale-blue lines spread beneath your skin like frozen veins.
MR 4 — Environmental Echo Your presence creates small, harmless changes around you. Frost gathers briefly on objects you touch and cold lingers where you stand.
MR 5+ — Mythic Signature Your nature becomes increasingly difficult to mistake for something ordinary. A halo of frost shimmers around you and tiny snowflakes sometimes drift through still air.

A new Schtick does not have to be an upgraded version of an earlier one. A character may develop several different manifestations representing different aspects of their Powers, Echo, Artifacts, experiences, or personality.

Using Schticks in Play

Schticks exist to help describe characters and their evolution. Use them when describing how a character enters a scene, activates a Power, becomes emotional, suffers injury, invokes an Artifact, or reaches a new stage of Mastery. They may also become recognizable features that friends, enemies, witnesses, or legends associate with that character. They remain narrative unless another rule explicitly gives them mechanics.

Schticks Are Not Powers

A Schtick cannot provide a free mechanical ability. A character whose eyes glow in darkness does not automatically gain Darkvision. A character surrounded by frost does not deal cold damage. A character who appears briefly translucent does not gain Phasing. A character whose voice sounds terrifying does not gain a bonus to Intimidation. If you want one of those effects, choose or acquire the appropriate Power.

Describe freely. Resolve mechanically through the rules.

Example: Schticks

The following examples show how different themes might manifest as Mastery grows. These are suggestions, not fixed lists.

Freeze

Rank Schtick Example
MR 1 — Minor Trait Your breath mists even in warm rooms.
MR 2 — Distinct Feature Your touch feels cold, and tears or sweat may crystallize briefly.
MR 3 — Defining Aspect Pale-blue lines spread beneath your skin like frozen veins.
MR 4 — Environmental Echo Frost gathers briefly on objects you touch, and cold lingers where you stand.
MR 5+ — Mythic Signature Fine snow sometimes drifts around you even beneath a clear sky.

Ruin

Rank Schtick Example
MR 1 — Minor Trait Your breath carries the faint scent of smoke.
MR 2 — Distinct Feature Sparks flicker at your lips, fingers, or eyes when emotion rises.
MR 3 — Defining Aspect Thin ember-lines glow beneath your skin, especially around scars or veins.
MR 4 — Environmental Echo Heat shimmer surrounds you, candles lean toward you, and ash drifts in still air.
MR 5+ — Mythic Signature Your silhouette sometimes appears wreathed in distant flame without anything actually burning.

Beast

Rank Schtick Example
MR 1 — Minor Trait Your eyes reflect light like an animal's in darkness.
MR 2 — Distinct Feature Your movements become unnervingly still, fluid, or predatory.
MR 3 — Defining Aspect Teeth, nails, posture, voice, or facial features take on a clearly bestial quality.
MR 4 — Environmental Echo Nearby animals become noticeably attentive, restless, or quiet when your power stirs.
MR 5+ — Mythic Signature For an instant, observers may glimpse the outline of something far larger and more primal moving with you.

Divine

Rank Schtick Example
MR 1 — Minor Trait Your eyes catch a faint blue gleam in darkness.
MR 2 — Distinct Feature A cold blue shimmer gathers around your scars, hands, or pupils when you focus.
MR 3 — Defining Aspect Your presence carries a visible blue radiance, like moonlight beneath the skin.
MR 4 — Environmental Echo The air around you dims and glows blue; dust, mist, or falling ash hangs briefly in your presence.
MR 5+ — Mythic Signature For brief moments, the space around you resembles sacred light from an age that no longer exists.

Example: Alaris Chooses Languages and Schticks

Every character speaks the Common Tongue and gains one additional language. For Elorians, this language is fixed as Elvish. Alaris therefore automatically learns Elvish through her Elorian Echo, connecting her directly to Elorian history, communities, and surviving traditions. Alaris is Mastery Rank 2 and therefore chooses two Schticks. Both are purely descriptive and grant no concealment, teleportation, movement, or defensive benefit.

Between the Steps

Sometimes Alaris appears to vanish for the smallest part of a movement. An observer sees where the step begins and where it ends, but a fragment between those moments seems to be missing from reality.

The Six Within

When Alaris channels one of her Powers, her eyes become completely black. Anyone looking closely can see the Six Constants burning faintly inside them like distant stars.

What this example shows

A Schtick should make a character recognizable without duplicating a Power as a free mechanical benefit.

Social Challenges optionally organize negotiations, intrigue, public arguments, and other meaningful conversations. They are not a separate dice or resource system.

Use the universal Training Roll: Attribute k MR, with Training Advantage and optional Training Crit from a fitting Profession. One meaningful exchange normally needs one check. Longer scenes may contain distinct tasks, but there is no fixed number of phases or mandatory Lead.

Shared Profession Procedure

  1. Describe the objective. Determine what the other person might plausibly agree to, reveal, or believe. Choose a fitting Attribute and a plausible Profession such as Courtier, Merchant, Spy, or Street Urchin, based on how the player approaches the exchange.
  2. Choose the comparison. An uncontested request, speech, or professional social task is a Standard Training Check against Task Level x 4, with optional predeclared Raises at +4 TN each. If a trained opponent actively challenges the attempt, use a Comparative Training Check: each side rolls once, with no Task TN or Raises.
  3. Resolve. Use Training Advantage and any available declared Training Crit on each eligible roll. For a Standard Check, success grants the basic outcome and its declared feasible Raise effects. For a Comparative Check, the higher result wins; a tie favors the defender or established position.

Social agency: A persuasive approach is not mind control. Success cannot compel an impossible concession or erase essential loyalties. Concrete leverage, evidence, and a credible proposal may change what is feasible, but do not automatically grant flat bonuses.

One Conversation — A City Gate

The captain listens to a traveler requesting entry. The GM sets Task Level 4 (Base TN 16). A negotiator with Courtier 4, Influence 4, MR 2 declares one Quality Raise, raising the Final TN to 20. They roll 4k2, rerolling eligible initial 1s–4s through Training Advantage. An outcome of 22 succeeds and secures the plausible assurance of future entry. 15 fails. There are no additional Free Raises. A fundamentally different offer may justify a new attempt; repeating the same pitch endlessly does not.

A Major Negotiation — The Prince's Troops

Find the real concern. A character uses Courtier 3 and Intellect at Base TN 12, declares one Insight Raise (Final TN 16), and discovers an additional supported fact: the prince fears leaving his capital defenseless.

Create a credible offer. Another uses Herald 3 to formalize an undertaking at Base TN 16, declaring one Quality Raise (Final TN 20) for a dependable proposal.

Ask for the troops. Diplomat 4 may attempt a feasible request at Base TN 20; a further Quality Raise would make it TN 24. If the prince actively opposes the negotiator with a credible trained trained method, replace the TN procedure with one Comparative Training Check per side, without Raises. No mandatory preparatory phase exists: credible prior evidence may already support the direct request.

Comparative Training Check — A False Courier

A character with Spy 3, Influence 4, MR 2 poses as a courier. A suspicious guard with City Watchman 2, Wits 4, MR 2 tries to expose the story. No setup Task TN is required: both roll 4k2, each using their Training Advantage. The courier obtains 22 and the guard 19, so the cover holds. If the guard rolls 24, the guard exposes the courier. A tie favors the inspecting guard. Neither participant declares Raises.

Shared Table Guidance

  • Cooperation: Characters may contribute distinct credible actions, each with its own purpose and consequences. There is no obligatory lead or fixed assistance bonus.
  • Raises: Only Standard Training Checks permit Raises. Declare their number before the roll (+4 TN each), and apply the approved effects on success. Training Rank grants no Free Raises and imposes no fixed Raise cap.
  • Consequences: Failure can change trust, available options, time, or risk. Fear Checks are not automatic.
  • Pacing: Use one comparison where one meaningful decision settles the matter. Use several distinct checks only when the fiction presents genuinely different tasks.

Every hero carries scars — some visible, others etched into the soul. Disadvantages are flaws, burdens, weaknesses, obligations, fears, curses, enemies, dependencies, or restrictions that make your character more complicated and more dangerous to play. They are not meant to make a character unplayable. They are meant to create pressure, hard choices, complications, and drama.

Open List Rule

The Disadvantages in this chapter are examples and templates. They are not a closed list. Players may create custom Disadvantages with GM approval.

When creating a custom Disadvantage, define:

  • what triggers it,
  • how often it matters,
  • what happens when it matters,
  • whether the character can resist it,
  • and how many Disadvantage Points it is worth.

A Disadvantage should be clear enough that both player and GM understand when it applies.

Disadvantage Rules

  • You may pick Disadvantages up to a maximum of 8 Disadvantage Points total.
  • Your maximum Disadvantage Points become your maximum Reroll Points.
  • After each Safe Haven Rest, you start at your maximum Reroll Points.

If a Disadvantage calls for a control roll, use:

Resolve k1

No Raises may be declared on this roll.

Rewarding Disadvantages

When a player actively roleplays a Disadvantage in a way that creates meaningful tension, risk, drama, sacrifice, or complication, the GM may allow that character to recover 1 Reroll Point. This should reward real play, not empty mention.

Good examples include:

  • acting on a fear even when it creates danger,
  • refusing an easy solution because of an oath,
  • accepting a complication because of a flaw,
  • exposing a weakness at a dramatic moment,
  • following an addiction, curse, obsession, or trauma when it matters,
  • allowing Hunted, Unluck, or a Physical Scar to shape the scene,
  • choosing a harder path because the Disadvantage genuinely matters.

A player cannot recover more Reroll Points than their maximum. The GM decides when a Disadvantage was played strongly enough to restore a Reroll Point.

Addiction (2 Points)

You are dependent on a physical, mental, magical, spiritual, or metaphysical substance, ritual, state, or contact to remain stable. This may be addiction, withdrawal, dependency, compulsion, or supernatural need.

Effect:

If you are denied the source of your Addiction:

Time Without Penalty
1 Tyhran Day –1d8 to all Attribute-based Training Check Pools
7 Tyhran Days –2d8 to all Attribute-based Training Check Pools
1 Lunar Month (44 Tyhran Days) –4d8 to all Attribute-based Training Check Pools
3 Lunar Months or more –8d8 to all Attribute-based Training Check Pools

When the Addiction is offered, threatened, denied, or becomes dangerous to pursue, the GM may call for a Resolve k1 control check. The GM states the trigger and TN before the roll:

  • TN 8 — Ordinary temptation or manageable withdrawal: the source is nearby, available, or missed under otherwise tolerable conditions.
  • TN 16 — Acute compulsion or severe withdrawal: a powerful trigger, prolonged denial, or a particularly dangerous opportunity to satisfy the need.

Use the fixed band that describes the actual situation, not the character's MR. This is an Attribute Check, not a Training Check; no Training Raises apply. The existing time-without penalties above remain in force on their stated schedule. On failure, the character suffers an appropriate complication, such as distraction, withdrawal, risky behavior, accepting a bad bargain, or exposing their weakness. Success means the character resists that specific trigger; it does not erase the Addiction or its ongoing penalties.

Examples:

  • A Sentinel requires sacred oil to regulate its systems.
  • A magic user needs Dreamdust to silence voices.
  • A believer is dependent on divine communion and suffers agony without prayer.
  • A blood-bound warrior craves battle or bloodshed.
  • A cursed oracle needs visions, dreams, or forbidden contact to remain stable.

Berserker’s Curse (2 Points)

You lose control when badly wounded, succumbing to blood-fury.

Trigger:
When you lose your second Health Level, and each time you lose another Health Level thereafter, make a Resolve k1 roll against TN 6. If one damage instance causes you to lose multiple Health Levels and crosses more than one qualifying threshold, make one test for each Health Level lost from the second onward. No Raises may be declared on this roll. On failure, you go Berserk for 1d8 / 2 rounds, rounded up.

While Berserk:

  • You gain +1d8 damage per Mastery Rank.
  • You must attack the nearest creature, friend or foe.
  • At the end of each round, repeat the Resolve k1 roll against TN 6 to regain control.

If you succeed, Berserk ends.

Hunted (1–3 Points)

Someone or something is hunting you and it will not stop. This may be a person, monster, faction, noble house, guild, cult, spirit, divine agent, demonic patron, family, government, or supernatural force. The examples below are not a closed list.

Points Threat Examples
1 A limited or personal threat A bounty hunter, rival, debt collector, betrayed lover, local guard captain
2 An organized threat with resources A cult, noble house, mercenary guild, criminal syndicate, church order
3 A powerful or far-reaching threat A demon lord, archwitch, archangel, ancient spirit, royal inquisition, planar hunter

Define:

  • who is hunting you,
  • why they are hunting you,
  • how much they know,
  • how far their reach extends,
  • whether they want capture, revenge, punishment, service, silence, or death.

Effect:
The GM may introduce chases, clues, agents, confrontations, traps, rumors, or social complications connected to the hunter. Hunted should create story pressure. It should not appear randomly just to punish the player.

Physical Scars (1–3 Points)

Your body bears lasting damage, weakness, mutation, instability, or limitation. Physical Scars are not limited to the examples below.

They may affect:

  • sight,
  • hearing,
  • sleep,
  • movement,
  • hands,
  • breathing,
  • stamina,
  • pain,
  • balance,
  • coordination,
  • appearance,
  • or physical reliability.
Example Flaw Points Effect
One-Eyed 1 −1 die to Ranged Attack Pools and sight-based Perception Pools.
One-Handed 2 You cannot dual wield or use a shield and one-handed weapon at the same time.
Heavy Sleeper 1 You do not wake from normal noise. You wake only when damaged, physically shaken, or directly disturbed.
Light Sleeper 1 You sleep poorly and may suffer complications during rests, watches, or exhaustion scenes.
Sleepless 2–3 You cannot sleep normally. Define with the GM how you recover during rests.
Chronic Pain 1–2 Under stress, the GM may require a Resolve k1 check (TN 8 for ordinary strain, TN 16 for acute pain) to remain focused. State the TN before the roll; no Training Raises. Failure causes an appropriate short-term pain complication; no unprinted permanent penalty.
Damaged Lungs 1–2 Smoke, poison gas, drowning, long chases, or exhaustion affect you more severely.
Trembling Hands 1–2 Fine manipulation, delicate tools, ranged precision, or spell focus may become harder under pressure.
Fragile Frame 3 Your Health Track has one fewer box on every level.

The important question is not whether the flaw appears on this list.

The important question is:

How does this complicate play, and how often does it matter?

Mental Restrictions (1–3 Points)

You are bound by your past, beliefs, trauma, instincts, compulsions, vows, fears, or personality. Mental Restrictions are not ordinary preferences. They must be strong enough to create real pressure in play. The examples below are not a closed list.

Oaths

  • No killing
  • Chivalric code
  • Always keep promises
  • Never abandon an ally
  • Never refuse a duel
  • Never lie
  • Never harm the helpless
  • Never break hospitality
  • Always repay debts

Fears

Fears should be handled like psychological limitations. A Fear must have a clear trigger and a clear consequence.

Examples:

  • Claustrophobia
  • Fear of fire
  • Fear of deep water
  • Fear of darkness
  • Fear of being restrained
  • Fear of undead
  • Fear of demons
  • Fear of divine symbols
  • Fear of mirrors
  • Fear of losing control
  • Fear of becoming a monster
  • Paranoia
  • Hatred for a group

Personality Traits

  • Arrogant — always needs to prove superiority
  • Coward — retreats or hesitates when seriously threatened
  • Vengeful — cannot forgive a serious offense
  • Gullible — easily moved by sad stories, pleading, or false innocence
  • In love with someone — acts irrationally when that person is in danger
  • Obsessive — cannot ignore a specific goal, clue, person, or mystery
  • Proud — cannot accept humiliation
  • Cruel — struggles to show mercy
  • Merciful — struggles to finish helpless enemies

Mental Restriction Rule

To act against your Mental Restriction, make a Resolve k1 roll. No Raises may be declared on this roll.

Difficulty TN Meaning Points
Easy 4 Minor resistance or mild discomfort 1
Normal 8 Strong internal conflict 2
Hard 12 Violates a core belief, fear, vow, or identity 3

On success, you may act against the Restriction for the moment. On failure, the Restriction creates a complication. This may mean hesitation, refusal, panic, retreat, escalation, social conflict, tactical risk, or another consequence agreed by the GM and player. A Mental Restriction should create drama and pressure. It should not remove the character from play every time it appears.

Unluck (1–3 Points)

You are cursed with misfortune. At the start of each session, the GM gains Misfortune Tokens based on your Unluck value.

The GM may spend a Misfortune Token to:

  • worsen the outcome of one of your failed rolls,
  • introduce an unlikely narrative obstacle,
  • create an inconvenient complication,
  • affect an ally caught in your bad luck,
  • or make an already bad situation worse.
Points Misfortune Tokens per Session
1 1d8 / 2, rounded up
2 1d8
3 2d8

Misfortune should complicate the story. It should not be used to invalidate player choices or turn success into failure.

Vulnerability (1-4 Points)

You are unusually susceptible to a specific harmful Special. Choose one eligible negative value-based Special. Add your Vulnerability value to the incoming Special before Special Negation. This only affects the Special when it is applied. It does not trigger again when the Special ticks. It does not add extra hits, extra stacks, or a separate Special. It does not make the Special harder to remove unless a rule explicitly says so.

Example:
If you have Vulnerability: Ruin(2) and an enemy applies Ruin(3) to you, you suffer Ruin(5) instead.

Eligible Specials:

Special Vulnerability Effect
Lacerate(X) When Lacerate is applied to you, increase its value by your Vulnerability value.
Ruin(X) When Ruin is applied to you, increase its value by your Vulnerability value.
Slow(X) When Slow is applied to you, increase its value by your Vulnerability value.
Hex(X) When Hex is applied to you, increase its value by your Vulnerability value.
Sundered(X) When Sundered is applied to you, increase its value by your Vulnerability value; the extra stacks affect subsequent eligible non-Spell hits under the normal Sundered rules.

Reroll Points — Fractures of Faith

Reroll Points represent the shattered, fragmented nature of the characters. Their memories, weaknesses, scars, and nightmares are not only burdens. They can also become a source of desperate strength.

Starting and Recovery

  • Your maximum Reroll Points equal your total Disadvantage Points.
  • You recover all Reroll Points after a Safe Haven Rest.
  • You cannot have more Reroll Points than your maximum.
  • The GM may allow you to recover 1 Reroll Point when you strongly roleplay a Disadvantage in a way that creates meaningful tension, risk, sacrifice, or complication.

This reward should be given for real consequences, not for simply mentioning the flaw.

Using Reroll Points

You may spend 1 Reroll Point to reroll all dice of one roll you make. You must keep the new result. You may also spend 1 Reroll Point to force the GM to reroll all dice of one roll they make. The GM must keep the new result. Reroll Points may be combined with other reroll effects unless a rule says otherwise.

You hesitate. Voices in your head. And yet — you try again.

Example: Disadvantages

The following examples show how a character might combine Disadvantages up to the maximum of 8 Disadvantage Points. These are not fixed packages. They only show how Disadvantages can create pressure, story hooks, and Reroll Points.

Example: Marked Fugitive

Disadvantage Points Trigger / Effect Narrative Hook
Hunted (Demonic Cult) 3 The GM may introduce cult agents, informants, ambushes, or social pressure connected to the hunter. Someone wants the character captured, silenced, or returned alive.
Addiction (Ritual Incense) 2 If denied the source, the character suffers the normal Addiction penalties over time. The character needs a nightly rite to remain stable.
Mental Restriction (Never Trust the Faithful of the Old Gods) 2 Acting against this restriction requires a Resolve k1 roll against the appropriate TN. Old betrayal makes trust in believers, temple servants, or keepers of the old rites difficult.
Unluck 1 The GM gains Misfortune Tokens according to the Unluck rules. Trouble finds the character at the worst possible time.

Total: 8 Points

Example: Broken Veteran

Disadvantage Points Trigger / Effect Narrative Hook
Physical Scar (Damaged Lungs) 2 Smoke, poison gas, drowning, long chases, or exhaustion may affect the character more severely. The war left wounds that never fully healed.
Hunted (Old War Enemy) 2 The GM may introduce pursuers, bounty notices, old rivals, or dangerous recognition. Someone from the past still wants revenge.
Mental Restriction (Never Abandon an Ally) 2 Leaving an ally behind requires a Resolve k1 roll against the appropriate TN. Loyalty is strength, but also a chain.
Berserker’s Curse 2 When the character loses their second Health Level, and each further Health Level thereafter, they risk losing control according to the Berserker’s Curse rules. Pain turns discipline into fury.

Total: 8 Points

Example: Cursed Wanderer

Disadvantage Points Trigger / Effect Narrative Hook
Vulnerability (Ruin) 4 Whenever Ruin(X) is applied to the character, increase the applied Ruin value by 4. Fire does not merely burn them; it awakens the curse.
Mental Restriction (Fear of Fire) 2 Acting calmly near dangerous flame requires a Resolve k1 roll against the appropriate TN. The character remembers burning, even when no fire is present.
Physical Scar (Trembling Hands) 1 Fine manipulation, delicate tools, ranged precision, or spell focus may become harder under pressure. The body still shakes from an old trauma.
Unluck 1 The GM gains Misfortune Tokens according to the Unluck rules. Misfortune follows like a shadow.

Total: 8 Points

Example: Alaris Chooses Disadvantages

Alaris takes the full 8 Disadvantage Points. Those points become her maximum Reroll Points, but every choice also creates a real complication.

Disadvantage Points How it matters
Lost Love: Liora 3 Her connection to Liora can override caution or immediate priorities.
Light Sleeper 2 Rest becomes fragile in unsafe or unfamiliar places.
Nightmares 1 Sleep may return her to memories, omens, or images she cannot control.
Vegetarian 2 Scarcity can turn a personal conviction into a survival problem.
What this example shows

A useful Disadvantage creates decisions and story pressure. It should not exist only to generate Reroll Points.

The Finished Character: Alaris

The final character should read as one connected plan rather than a collection of unrelated high values.

Final element Alaris
Mastery Rank 2
Core role Mobile melee skirmisher
Total Evade 17 from the MR baseline and her artifacts
Armor 2 from Mastery Rank soak
Health per Bar 16 from Vitality 4 × 4
Fear Starts at 0; accumulated Fear remains until Safe Haven Rest.
Main weapon Moonlight Greatsword (Artifact Level 1): 5d8 Weapon Damage (4d8 Greatsword + 1d8 Artifact), Inherent Finesse, Precision(2)
Assigned Stones Agility 1 and Vitality 1
Echo Imprints Catfall (Agility), Living Warmth (Vitality)

Moonlight Greatsword - Inherent Finesse: This named Artifact retains the normal Greatsword's 4d8 starting weapon damage and Precision(2), while its own Inherent Ability: Finesse permits Agility for the Attack Roll (not for damage). At Artifact Level 1 its +1d8 Artifact Weapon Damage produces 5d8 total Weapon Damage. Inherent Finesse is not an additional Power, a purchased Special, or a fourth Artifact Base Value.

Her combat rhythm

  1. Reach a useful melee position through normal movement, a purchased Movement Power if available, or an Agility Stone option. Catfall offers no combat movement bonus.
  2. Choose between direct damage and applying Sundered for the group.
  3. Let high Evade answer ordinary direct attacks.
  4. Reserve Phasing for the most dangerous hits.
  5. Spend Stones when movement, survival, or Special removal cannot wait.
What the complete example teaches

A strong Mastery character does not need to cover every role. Alaris has a clear offensive purpose, a clear defensive plan, and several supporting choices that express the same identity.
